name: Sillaway v. Brandon Crossroads Bowl, Inc.
hold_reasons: fidelity flag: The opinion is a Florida case applying Florida Statutes § 768.125 only; there is no reference to or equivalence with Georgia's O.C.G.A. in the opinion, making this an unsupported/incorrect insertion. (drafted text at issue: "O.C.G.A. equivalent section 768.125, Florida Statutes")

entry.name: Sillaway v. Brandon Crossroads Bowl, Inc.
entry.synopsis: In a wrongful death and personal injury action under Florida's dram shop statute, O.C.G.A. equivalent section 768.125, Florida Statutes, plaintiffs sued a bowling alley alleging it knowingly served alcohol to a habitually addicted patron who then drove and caused a fatal crash. Years later, after deposition testimony indicated a different occupant had been driving, plaintiffs sought to amend to allege that one of two other men was the driver and that the vendor knew each of them was habitually addicted. The Second District held the amendment did not relate back under Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.190(c), reasoning that vendor liability under section 768.125 is derivative rather than vicarious and that substituting a different alleged driver changed the core factual allegation, requiring proof of the vendor's knowledge of a different person's addiction, and thus presented a new factual narrative rather than a new legal theory built on the original one. The court distinguished cases permitting relation back where a plaintiff merely corrected the identity of the employee whose negligence supported a vicarious liability claim against an unchanged institutional defendant. Affirmed.
entry.why: The decision draws a line under Kopel between amendments that add new legal theories to the same factual narrative, which relate back, and amendments that change the core facts underlying a defendant's derivative liability, which do not, in the specific context of dram shop claims where the identity of the intoxicated person defines the vendor's alleged knowledge.

additional_holdings.synopsis: As an independent, alternative ground, the court held that even if the amended complaint had related back, the trial court acted within its discretion in denying the amendment because of unfair prejudice. It pointed to the eight-year gap since the crash, the nearly six-year gap since suit was filed, the four-year delay after the deposition that first suggested a different driver, the loss of critical evidence, and the death of a key witness who was never deposed. The court found no abuse of discretion in denying amendment and proceeding to summary judgment on the original complaint.
additional_holdings.why: It confirms that a trial court may deny a late amendment on prejudice grounds even when the relation-back test would otherwise be satisfied, making the timing of an amendment after new facts emerge in discovery independently consequential.
